In summary, a comprehensive and detailed conclusive statement would be that
the evidence is insufficient to determine whether stereotactic radiosurgery (SRS) or stereotactic body radiation therapy (SBRT) improves survival or local control for patients with chordomas.
the evidence is not yet available to determine the role of stereotactic radiosurgery in the treatment of chordomas.
the evidence for the use of stereotactic radiosurgery (SRS) and stereotactic hypofractionated radiotherapy (SHR) for cranial base or cervical chordomas is limited and inconclusive.
A comprehensive summary for our work would be that
we have shown that there is no evidence to support the notion of an increased risk of developing a second primary malignancy (SPM) in the head and neck region following treatment with proton therapy.

we have demonstrated that stereotactic radiosurgery (SRS) and hypofractionation are safe and effective treatments for recurrent or residual cranial base and cervicocranial chordomas, and that the addition of surgery to SRS and hypofractioned stereotactic radiotherapies (HSRT) is associated with a better outcome.
the results of SRS and HSRT for residual and recurrent cranial base chordoma are excellent, with low rates of local recurrence, acceptable complication rates, and good overall survival.
The main takeaway from our work is that
the majority of chordoma patients are not cured by radiation therapy, and that the risk of radiation-induced malignancy is significant.
the use of hypofractionated radiation therapy (RT) in the management of chordomas is feasible, with a high rate of local control and acceptable rates of toxicity.
, for patients with chordomas of the skull base, the use of a hypofractionated regimen of SRS or SRT can result in excellent local control rates with acceptable toxicity profiles.
